Usually, but not necessarily, in any one symbol sentence (equation) or instruction, different letters or different symbols represent different unknown numbers. A value is said to solve a symbol sentence (or an equation) if substituting the value into the sentence (equation) satisfies it, i.e. results in a true statement .
3 12
For example, we can say that 4 solves the symbol sentence (equation) 9 – = + 1 (or 9 – x = x + 1) because it is a true statement that 9 – 4 = 4 + 1. We say that 4 satisfies the symbol sentence (equation) 9 – = + 1 (or 9 – x = x + 1).

Each unit in our primary maths curriculum aligns both in sequence and recommended duration to the units in the Curriculum Prioritisation materials from the National Centre of Excellence in the Teaching of Mathematics (NCETM).
They also correspond to the specific statements within the ready-to-progress criteria within the Department for Education’s non-statutory guidance .
Read more about this in our blog: Supporting the use of NCETM Curriculum Prioritisation materials .

We build in problem solving throughout units whilst also drawing specific attention to it within particular lessons that focus on features of solving specific types of problem and exploring the efficacy of different methods.

Coherence is at the centre of the design of the materials, and the key threads that run throughout reflect the structure of the National Curriculum, allowing teachers to track the development of key knowledge and skills. Lesson materials include slide decks, videos, worksheets and quizzes.
Everything available from Oak National Academy is quality checked. All resources are free to download, and adaptable to make them bespoke to the needs of pupils. Visit the Oak National Academy website to learn more.

results.title: Solving Two-Step Equations
excerpts:
A two-step equation is an algebraic equation with two operations in it that requires two steps to solve. To solve equations with multiple operations, we need to first determine what order to do those operations in.
Now, we perform the inverse of the first operation we did when evaluating. That was multiplication and its inverse is division.
3 x 3 = 15 3 x = 5
In general, we want to perform addition or subtraction first, then perform multiplication or division.
This video by CK-12 provides an example of solving two-step equations.
Solve 4 x − 9 = 11.
Solution: We need to undo two operations. First, we do the inverse of subtraction and add 9 to both sides.
4 x − 9 = 11 + 9 + 9 _ perform addition or subtraction 4 x = 20
The inverse of multiplication is division, so we divide both sides by 4 to solve for x .
4 x 4 = 20 4 perform multiplication or division x = 5
Solve 18 = 6 − 2 5 y .
Solution: Even though the term with the variable is not first, we can still follow the same steps.
18 = 6 − 2 5 y − 6 − 6 _ 12 = − 2 5 y − 5 2 ⋅ 12 = − 5 2 ⋅ − 2 5 y − 30 = y
Check your answer: 6 − 2 5 ( − 30 ) = 6 + 12 = 18
This video by Mathispower4u demonstrates how to solve two-step equations that include fractions.
Solve x − 2 3 = 5.
Solution: This is a linear equation. We can see this if we divide 3 into each of the terms in the numerator: 1 3 x − 2 3 = 5 . However, instead of dividing 3 into each of the terms, it is helpful to multiply both sides of the equation by 3 to undo the division by 3 in the denominator.
